learn: Approximating action values q̂(s, a, θ) = θᵀφ(s, a)
Semi-gradient SARSA with a fully worked update (the dino game)
Maximisation bias with approximation, and Double Q-learning
intro.why: DQN was the first method to learn control directly from raw pixels across many Atari games. It is Q-learning plus a neural network plus two stabilisers, each of which answers a specific failure mode of approximate off-policy bootstrapping.

sections.title: Action-value function approximation
sections.plain: Give each state–action pair features and score it with one shared weight vector.
sections.body:
To act without a model we approximate action values. Folding the action into the feature vector lets one weight vector cover every state–action pair:

$$\hat q(s,a,\theta) = \theta^\top\phi(s,a),\qquad \theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha\big[U_t - \hat q(S_t,A_t,\theta)\big]\nabla\hat q(S_t,A_t,\theta)$$

For linear $\hat q$, $\nabla\hat q = \phi(s,a)$. Alternatively a network can output one value per action from the state alone (as DQN does).

Running example: the dino game. Features $\phi = [\text{bias}, \text{obstacle close}, \text{jump?}]$. $\theta = [1.0, 0.5, 1.0]$, a second network $\theta' = [0.1, 0.3, 1.0]$, $\gamma = 0.2$, $\alpha = 0.9$. Transition $(S_1, a{=}0, r{=}2, S_2, a'{=}0)$ with $\phi(S_1,0) = [1,0,0]$, $\phi(S_2,0) = [1,1,0]$, $\phi(S_2,1) = [1,1,1]$. Then $\hat q(S_1,0) = 1.0$, $\hat q(S_2,0) = 1.5$, $\hat q(S_2,1) = 2.5$.

sections.title: Semi-gradient SARSA: a worked update
sections.plain: Target = reward + γ × value of the action actually taken next.
sections.body:
$$\theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha\big[R + \gamma\hat q(S',A',\theta) - \hat q(S,A,\theta)\big]\phi(S,A)$$

Worked (on-policy). Next action actually taken $a' = 0$: target $= 2 + 0.2\cdot1.5 = 2.30$; $\delta = 2.30 - 1.0 = 1.30$; $\theta \leftarrow [1.0, 0.5, 1.0] + 0.9\cdot1.30\cdot[1,0,0] = [2.17, 0.5, 1.0]$. Only $\theta_1$ changes, because only the first feature is active in $(S_1, 0)$.

Episodic semi-gradient SARSA with tile coding solves continuous tasks such as mountain car (an underpowered car must rock back and forth to climb a hill). In ex1, with 8 tilings and zero (optimistic) initial values, episode length drops from 1,704 steps to about 120–150 within 100–200 episodes.

sections.title: Q-learning with function approximation
sections.plain: Target = reward + γ × the best next action's value; off-policy, and riskier with approximation.
sections.body:
$$\theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha\big[R + \gamma\max_{a'}\hat q(S',a',\theta) - \hat q(S,A,\theta)\big]\phi(S,A)$$

Worked (off-policy). $\max\{1.5, 2.5\} = 2.5$; target $= 2 + 0.2\cdot2.5 = 2.50$; $\delta = 1.50$; $\theta \leftarrow [2.35, 0.5, 1.0]$.

With approximation, Q-learning combines all three elements of the deadly triad (approximation, bootstrapping, off-policy), so it has no general convergence guarantee and can diverge. SARSA (on-policy) with linear features is much better behaved (it may chatter near a good solution but doesn't diverge).

sections.title: Maximisation bias and Double Q with features
sections.plain: Choose the next action with one set of weights and score it with another.
sections.body:
Suppose the true values are $q(S_2,0) = q(S_2,1) = 2.0$; the honest target is $2 + 0.2\cdot2.0 = 2.40$. Our noisy estimates are 1.5 and 2.5; the max picks 2.5 and the target is 2.50, an overestimate. Because the same weights choose and evaluate, errors compound through bootstrapping.

Double Q. Select with $\theta$: $a^* = \arg\max_a\hat q(S_2,a,\theta) = 1$ (2.5 > 1.5). Evaluate with $\theta'$: $\hat q(S_2,1,\theta') = 0.1 + 0.3 + 1.0 = 1.40$. Target $= 2 + 0.2\cdot1.40 = 2.28$; $\delta = 1.28$; $\theta \leftarrow [2.152, 0.5, 1.0]$. The roles of the two networks are swapped over time.

sections.title: Deep Q-networks: experience replay
sections.plain: Store past transitions and train on random mini-batches to break correlations and reuse data.
sections.body:
Replace $\theta^\top\phi$ with a deep network (DQN: convolutional layers over the last four stacked frames, one output per action). Two problems appear: consecutive samples are highly correlated (adjacent frames), and nonlinear approximation with off-policy bootstrapped updates can diverge.

Experience replay stores the last N transitions $(s,a,r,s')$ in a buffer $\mathcal D$, overwriting the oldest, and trains on uniformly random mini-batches:

  • breaks correlations between consecutive samples (closer to i.i.d. SGD);
  • reuses each transition many times (data efficiency);
  • smooths the training distribution over many past behaviours.

Replay makes learning necessarily off-policy (the data came from older policies), which suits Q-learning. Prioritised replay samples transitions with large TD error more often, correcting the induced bias with importance weights.

sections.title: Target networks and Double DQN
sections.plain: Compute targets with a frozen copy of the network, updated only occasionally.
sections.body:
Target network. Compute targets with a frozen copy $\theta^-$, synchronised to $\theta$ every $C$ steps:

$$L(\theta) = \mathbb E_{(s,a,r,s')\sim\mathcal D}\Big[\big(r + \gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a';\theta^-) - Q(s,a;\theta)\big)^2\Big]$$

Without it, every gradient step also moves the target (the network chases itself). Between syncs, each phase is an ordinary regression to fixed targets.

Double DQN applies the decoupling with networks already present: the online network selects, the target network evaluates:

$$y = r + \gamma\,Q\big(s', \arg\max_{a'}Q(s',a';\theta);\ \theta^-\big)$$

Code example ex2 (a tiny NumPy DQN on a point-mass task): both a full DQN and naive online Q-learning with the same network reach the goal in about 13 steps, but the naive learner's Q-value for the start state explodes to around 10⁵, while DQN's stays near the true −12.5. The greedy policy can survive while the values are meaningless, until it no longer does on harder tasks.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Later improvements (combined in "Rainbow"): dueling architectures (separate V and advantage streams), multi-step returns, distributional value estimates, noisy networks for exploration, prioritised replay.
  • DQN handles discrete actions only; continuous actions need actor–critic methods (DDPG, TD3, SAC; M11).
  • Reward clipping and frame skipping in the original Atari work were engineering choices that matter for reproduction.
  • Huber loss limits gradients from large TD errors, a further stabiliser.

code.title: Linear control: the dino updates and mountain car
code.explain: Reproduces the three worked targets (2.30, 2.50, 2.28) and weight updates, then trains semi-gradient SARSA with 8 tilings on mountain car and prints episode lengths.
mistakes: Updating weights of features that were inactive.
Using a step size not divided by the number of tilings.
code.notes: Zero initial values are optimistic here (all rewards are −1), which drives exploration without ε.
code.code:
"""Approximate control with linear features: the dino worked updates, then semi-gradient SARSA on mountain car.

q_hat(s, a, theta) = theta . phi(s, a); semi-gradient update theta += alpha * delta * phi(s, a).
"""
import numpy as np
th, th2 = np.array([1.0, 0.5, 1.0]), np.array([0.1, 0.3, 1.0])
g, a, r = 0.2, 0.9, 2.0
phi = {("S1", 0): np.array([1, 0, 0.]), ("S2", 0): np.array([1, 1, 0.]), ("S2", 1): np.array([1, 1, 1.])}
q = lambda w, s, act: w @ phi[(s, act)]
print("q(S1,0) =", q(th, "S1", 0), " q(S2,0) =", q(th, "S2", 0), " q(S2,1) =", q(th, "S2", 1))
for name, nxt in [("SARSA (a'=0)", q(th, "S2", 0)), ("Q-learning (max)", max(q(th, "S2", 0), q(th, "S2", 1))),
                  ("Double Q (select th, evaluate th')", q(th2, "S2", int(np.argmax([q(th, "S2", 0), q(th, "S2", 1)]))))]:
    target = r + g * nxt; d = target - q(th, "S1", 0)
    print(f"{name:<36} target {target:.2f}  delta {d:.2f}  theta -> {np.round(th + a * d * phi[('S1', 0)], 3)}")
print("honest target if both true next values were 2.0:", r + g * 2.0)

# --- semi-gradient SARSA with tile coding on mountain car (classic continuous control benchmark)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
NT, NB = 8, 8                                   # 8 tilings of 8x8 over (position, velocity)
def tiles(x, v):
    xs, vs = (x + 1.2) / 1.7 * NB, (v + 0.07) / 0.14 * NB
    return [t * (NB + 1) ** 2 + int(xs + t / NT) * (NB + 1) + int(vs + 3 * t / NT % 1) for t in range(NT)]
W = np.zeros((3, NT * (NB + 1) ** 2))
def qv(x, v, act): return W[act, tiles(x, v)].sum()
def step(x, v, act):
    v = np.clip(v + 0.001 * (act - 1) - 0.0025 * np.cos(3 * x), -0.07, 0.07); x = x + v
    if x < -1.2: x, v = -1.2, 0.0
    return x, v, x >= 0.5
alpha, eps, lengths = 0.5 / NT, 0.0, []
for ep in range(200):
    x, v = rng.uniform(-0.6, -0.4), 0.0
    act = int(np.argmax([qv(x, v, b) for b in range(3)])); n = 0
    while n < 5000:
        n += 1; x2, v2, done = step(x, v, act)
        tl = tiles(x, v)
        if done: W[act, tl] += alpha * (-1 - W[act, tl].sum()); break
        a2 = int(np.argmax([qv(x2, v2, b) + rng.random() * 1e-9 for b in range(3)]))
        W[act, tl] += alpha * (-1 + qv(x2, v2, a2) - W[act, tl].sum())
        x, v, act = x2, v2, a2
    lengths.append(n)
print("\nmountain car, steps per episode (optimistic zero init, greedy):",
      " ".join(f"ep{e+1}:{lengths[e]}" for e in (0, 1, 4, 19, 49, 99, 199)))

code.title: A tiny DQN vs naive online Q-learning
code.explain: A 2-32-3 ReLU network trained with replay (buffer 5,000, batch 32) and a target network synced every 200 steps, compared with online updates on consecutive samples; reports steps to goal and the predicted value of the start state.
mistakes: Judging stability by the greedy policy alone.
code.notes: Gradient clipping is applied in both, so the difference comes from replay and the target network.
code.output:
DQN (replay + target net)   steps to goal, last 50 episodes:  13.4 | predicted Q(start) per seed: [-10.9 -12.1 -12.6]
naive online Q-learning     steps to goal, last 50 episodes:  13.3 | predicted Q(start) per seed: [215721.9 122885.  292841.8]
True Q(start) for a ~13-step path with gamma 0.99: -12.5.
Both greedy policies reach the goal (only the ranking of actions matters), but without replay and a target
network the Q-values themselves blow up: the network chases its own moving, correlated targets.
